passage:
"Vandana, why are you taking that photo eleven times?" Madhuri asked from the bed.
"Because the first ten make my hair look flat. Hold on, I'm cropping out the dirty cups."
"There are dirty cups?"
"Exactly. Nobody needs to know." Vandana typed a caption, deleted it, typed another: "monday mood 🙂". Then she stuck a sleepy-cat meme in the corner.
"That's a happy caption on a tired face."
"It's a joke, didi. Everyone in my class posts the cat one. It means we all hate Mondays."
"So it says you're with them."
"Kind of." Vandana paused. "Honestly I had a rotten day. But that's not what this is for." She pressed post and put the phone face down.

qa.q: What did Vandana crop out of the photo?
qa.a: She cropped out the dirty cups.

qa.q: What might Vandana be feeling as she posts a cheerful caption?
qa.a: Most likely she is covering a rotten day with a joke, since she admits it aloud, though she may also just want to join her class's cat meme and feel she belongs.

qa.q: What could Madhuri say next to keep Vandana talking?
qa.a: She could ask about the rotten day without criticising the post, so Vandana can share the parts the photo left out. 🙂

qa.q: How does Madhuri's view of the post differ from her classmates' view?
qa.a: Madhuri saw the tired face and the tidying, so the caption looks mismatched to her, while classmates only see the finished cat meme and may read it as a shared Monday joke.

grounding: A teen frames and edits a photo and meme to signal belonging and mood, showing a presented self rather than the whole day.

passage: Last year I thought a good selfie needed twenty tries and three filters. My friend Tanuja and I had a private group where we posted only our funniest edits: Tanuja's face on a potato, my face on a sad monsoon crow. Those memes were the best part of my day, and we never shared the ordinary photos. Then Tanuja stayed at my place after a cousin's wedding and scrolled through my page. "You look like you're always at a party," she said. I laughed, but I looked at my grid afterwards and it did show a sparkling girl I didn't quite know. I still post memes. I just leave a few plain photos in too. - Nikita

qa.q: What did Nikita and Tanuja post in their private group?
qa.a: They posted only their funniest edits, such as Tanuja's face on a potato and Nikita's face on a sad monsoon crow.

qa.q: What did Nikita feel when she looked at her own grid after Tanuja's remark?
qa.a: She felt a little unsettled, since the grid showed a sparkling girl she didn't quite know, though she also laughed, so she may have taken the remark partly as a compliment.

qa.q: What small change did Nikita make, and why might it help?
qa.a: She added a few plain photos among the memes, which keeps the humour while showing more of her ordinary life.

qa.q: How might Tanuja have meant her comment?
qa.a: It could be admiration, or a gentle observation that the page shows only parties. Tanuja's own edits were chosen too, so she may be noticing something familiar. 🙂

grounding: A teen looks back on curating memes and selfies as a chosen, framed self that leaves out ordinary life.

passage:
Photography club note - Nilesh (teacher in charge), Class 11
The brief this month was "a week in my life," seven photos. Samir submitted seven selfies: cricket ground, birthday cake, beach, new shoes, each with a wide grin and bright edits.
They were technically good. But when the club looked at them, one student said, "Your life looks like an advert."
Samir laughed it off. Then, after everyone left, he showed me an eighth photo he hadn't submitted: his desk at night, a pile of maths papers, a cold cup of tea, a lamp.
"That's most of my week," he said. "But nobody posts that."
I told him the seven were honest too, just chosen. The eighth was also chosen, just differently. Both are a presented self.
He asked if he could submit all eight. The club voted the desk photo the most striking of the month.

qa.q: How many selfies did Samir submit at first?
qa.a: Samir submitted seven selfies.

qa.q: What might Samir have been feeling when he showed the eighth photo?
qa.a: He seemed a little vulnerable and relieved to show a truer side, after laughing off the "advert" comment.

qa.q: What did Nilesh help Samir understand?
qa.a: That every photo is chosen and framed, so both the bright selfies and the desk photo present a self rather than the full picture.

qa.q: How might the club members have felt seeing the desk photo?
qa.a: They probably found it relatable and striking, since most of their weeks also include tired desks that nobody posts.

grounding: The teacher's note shows a teenager curating photos to present a bright self, and recognising posted images as chosen, not a full picture.

passage:
Saturday
Took forty-three selfies before the farewell party to get one good one. Forty-three! In the end I posted the one where my hair looked right and the light hid the pimple. Caption: "last day, best day ✨".
Honestly, the last day wasn't the best day. I cried in the bathroom because I'm going to miss everyone.
Then Nilesh posted a meme of our whole class: our faces stuck onto the cast of that old college film, with our class teacher as the principal. I laughed so hard. It felt more like us than any selfie.
It made me think. My selfie shows a girl who had a perfect day. The meme shows a class that's a bit of a mess and loves each other. The meme's closer to the truth.
Might post the bathroom-crying version next year. Maybe.
- Binita

qa.q: How many selfies did Binita take before the party?
qa.a: Binita took forty-three selfies.

qa.q: What was Binita feeling on the last day?
qa.a: Binita felt sad and nostalgic, crying in the bathroom because of missing everyone, even though the post said "best day."

qa.q: What would you advise Binita about posting next year?
qa.a: Choose images that feel true, like the class meme, and remember that a post is always a chosen version, not the whole day.

qa.q: How might Nilesh's classmates have seen his meme?
qa.a: They probably felt amused and connected, seeing their messy, affectionate class in a shared joke.

grounding: The diary shows a teenager curating a selfie that hides mixed feelings, and a group meme signalling humour and belonging.

passage: The temple fair in Sudha's kasba had been a long, hot day: the giant wheel broke down twice, her sandal strap snapped, and she spent an hour helping her uncle at the bangle stall. That night, on the charpai, she scrolled through sixty photos and chose three. A selfie with cotton candy, lit gold by the sunset. The giant wheel from below, looking enormous. And a funny edit of her cousin Charu in a paper crown with cartoon sparkles, captioned "queen of the mela 👑". Within an hour, classmates from town commented: "so jealous", "best day ever?" Charu, lying beside her, read the comments aloud and snorted. "Best day ever? You cried about the sandal." Sudha grinned. "Nobody wants the sandal." Then she paused. "Do you mind the crown one?" Charu shook her head. "I love it. Keep it." Sudha put the phone away, still smiling, the snapped sandal under the charpai.

qa.q: How many photos did Sudha choose from the sixty?
qa.a: Sudha chose three of the sixty photos.

qa.q: What was Sudha feeling while choosing the photos?
qa.a: Sudha seems happy and playful picking the bright moments, maybe a bit proud of the edits; the tiring parts like the snapped sandal weren't gone, just left out. 🙂

qa.q: What did Sudha get right about the photo of Charu?
qa.a: Sudha asked Charu whether she minded the crown edit before keeping it up, which respected Charu's say over her own image.

qa.q: How might the classmates see Sudha's day compared with Charu?
qa.a: The classmates saw a golden 'best day ever', while Charu, who was there, knew about the heat, the broken wheel and the sandal.

grounding: It shows a teenager curating fair photos and edits to present a fun, glowing self, while the full day was more mixed than the posts.
